Subject: EXCERPTS OF THE NORWEGIAN PRESS MONDAY 19 DECEMBER



 

 

 


 
EXCERPTS OF THE NORWEGIAN PRESS, MONDAY 19 DECEMBER 2022

 



 

POLITICAL, MILITARY AND GENERAL

 

WAR IN UKRAINE

Opinion: Based on opinion last week from Lt-Col Geir Hågen Karlsen with the Norwegian Staff Academy of a protracted war, Aftenposten concludes its leader on Saturday with: NATO members must clearly show as much patience as Ukraine itself has done. Russia s aggression must not be rewarded. Ukraine needs peace, but it must be on the country s own terms. Meanwhile, VG today fully understands the negative reactions from Ukrainians in Norway to Peace Initiative 2022 where inter alia LO Oslo (ignoring advice from LO leader Peggy Flesvik not to participate) and Red Party demonstrated outside the Parliament on Saturday urging Ukraine to seek Christmas peace, truce and negotiations with Russia. The newspaper is of the opinion that the only reason imperial Russia would want a ceasefire would be to re-group for a new offensive. VG assumes that the peace initiative is for democracy and freedom but points out that neither can be achieved by Ukraine laying down arms while Russian troops are still an invasion force. (Aft 17/12 p2(leader); VG 19/12 pp2(leader) & 30-31)

Aftenposten: Halvor Hegtun makes another attempt at trying to understand Putin, this time with focus on some strange comments he made during his recent visit to Kirgizstan (17/12 p3; also, DB pp1 & 8-10); Gina Grieg Riisnæs reports on life in Kherson, now being bombed regularly by its former occupiers (17/12 pp22-24; 19/12 pp6-8)

Elsewhere: (Aft 19/12 pp30-31; Da 19/12 p16; VG 17/12 pp36-37; 19/12 pp10 & 20-25; DB 17/12 pp6 & 12; 19/12 pp2-3, 4-5 & 6)

 

FURTHER MODERNISATION OF NORWAY S AIR DEFENCE

The Norwegian Defence Materiel Agency has signed a contract with German Rheinmetall for the upgrade of electro-optical sensors in the Norwegian Advanced Surface to Air Missile System (NASAMS). The value of the contract is around NOK 190m. The contract includes an upgrade of the current analogue sensor system to a new digital sensor system. NASAMS is a mobile, modular and highly accurate air defence system used by both the Norwegian Army and the Air Force. The system consists inter alia of launch units with missiles, command and control stations, radars and electro-optical sensors. The sensors to be upgraded are fitted on all-terrain vehicles and search for hostile threats in the air and on the ground, both in light and in the dark, using a TV camera and heat signature (infrared). The sensors also measure the distance to the target with a laser. The work to increase our national capacity against long-range precision weapons is ongoing and the modernisation of the current NASAMS is one of several measures aimed at strengthening Norway s air defence. The war in Ukraine has highlighted the need and importance of air defence. We have also recently signed a contract for the purchase of hand-held air defence weapons for the Army, to strengthen our ability to protect ourselves, says defence minister Bjørn Arild Gram. Upgraded sensors for the NASAMS will be continuously delivered to the Army and Air Force from the first half of 2025. (NMoD)

 

Q&A IN WESTERN SAHARA

Foreign minister Anniken Huitfeldt replies to written question no. 675 (2022-2023) from Freddy André Øvstegård (Socialist Left) on the Norwegian ship Heenvliet that was heading Western Sahara on charter (see PS of 9/12): Norway has officially advised against trade and other commercial activities in Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara since 2007, to prevent violations of international law, and in line with UN work to contribute to a solution to the conflict. Despite this, the Norwegian ship Heenvliet is on its way to Western Sahara with an estimated arrival of 11 December, according to Bergens Tidende of 8 December. What does the foreign minister think about such violations of official advice? Huitfeldt: The Norwegian authorities are keen to avoid actions that could be perceived as legitimising the situation in Western Sahara. Norway s precautionary stance is therefore firmly established. This is in the form of a general advice against trade, resource exploitation and other forms of business activity that are not in accordance with the interests of the Sahrawis and can consequently contribute to violations of international law. Morocco does not exercise internationally recognised sovereignty over Western Sahara, and thus does not have the right to exploit Western Sahara s natural resources as if they were their own. Our advice is a clear call to private actors to exercise caution and social responsibility when considering activity in the Western Sahara. It is also important to note that there is no legally binding ban on exports and commercial activities aimed at Western Sahara, nor UN sanctions or restrictive measures from the EU which involve export restrictions or other forms of restrictions related to commercial activities. (MFA)

 

MORE SUPPORT TO NATURE CONSERVATION

From the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in Montreal, climate & environment minister Espen Barth Eide announced that Norway was allocating a further NOK 120m to projects that will kick-start the implementation of a new nature agreement. The total funding needed to deliver on the global ambitions for the conservation and sustainable management of nature is estimated to be 5-8 times higher than current funding. In order to halt and reverse the loss of nature, there is therefore a need for significantly increased funding, both by countries stepping up their own efforts, and by banks, private companies and financial institutions contributing. In addition to new funding, environmentally damaging subsidies must be phased out, the Ministry says in a press release. (&).

Norway is the world s 5th largest country measured in aid to nature conservation. This includes the Norwegian rainforest initiative, in addition to aid for the conservation of marine areas and sustainable agriculture. Norway also puts considerable effort into mobilising funding from other countries, companies and the financial sector. An example of this is the mobilisation of USD 1.5bn for rainforest conservation through the LEAF coalition. If we are to solve the nature crisis, everyone must contribute more, including Norway. That is why the government will increase aid significantly until 2026, Barth Eide says. (&). (Press release; e24.no; Aft 19/12 p14)

 

WEEKLY REPORT ON NORWAY IN THE UN SECURITY COUNCIL

In week 49 the UN Security Council discussed: Iraq, Syria, DR Congo, Ukraine, Sudan, the Golan Heights, Central Africa, humanitarian exemptions in UN sanction regies.

Monday 5 December: Half-yearly meeting on UN ISIL investigation team (Unitad), with briefing by leader Christian Ritscher. Broad support for Unitad s core mandate, though some dissatisfaction that evidence has not been shared with the Iraqi authorities due to Iraqi laws and use of death sentence. Norway urged Iraq to temporarily suspend capital punishment in order to make progress. Norway also requested Unitad to continue prioritising the needs of survivors and to ensure an age and gender perspective in further work. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Open meeting and closed consultations on the elimination of Syria s chemical weapons programme. Read Norway s statement here.

6 December: Closed meeting with troop and police contributors to Monusco in DR Congo ahead of a mandate renewal later this month. Same day: Open meeting on the humanitarian situation in Ukraine called by France and Mexico. UN emergency aid coordinator Martin Griffiths painted a dire picture. Apart from Russia, members expressed considerable concern, particularly for the situation of children. Norway strongly condemned Russia s war of aggression with particular emphasis on the consequences of destroyed schools and health facilities for children and the Ukrainian civilian population. Norway also expressed concern about reports that Ukrainian children had been forcibly moved to Russia for adoption. Read Norway s statement here.

7 December: Open meeting and closed consultations on Sudan and Unitams, with briefing from the head of the sanctions committee for Sudan (1591), Ghana's UN ambassador, Agyeman. The meeting was characterised by new optimism after the civilian and military authorities in Sudan signed a new framework agreement on 5 December which may open up the formation of a new civilian government and a two-year transitional phase until the holding of democratic elections. Most of the council's members, including Norway, expressed concern that the humanitarian crisis in the country was worsening. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Closed meeting with troop and police contributors to Undof/Untso (Golan Heights). Norway supports Undof/Untso and the UN s role in continued monitoring of the ceasefire agreement.

8 December: Closed consultations on Undof (Golan Heights) before expected new mandate later this month. Same day: Half-yearly briefing and closed consultations on Unoca in Central Africa. Norway praised Unoca for its work and also expressed concern about the situation in eastern DR Congo, Chad and Cameroon, as well as about the food security situation in the region. Read Norway s statement here.

9 December: Meeting on the situation in DR Congo, Monusco and sanctions regime with briefings by UN special representative Bintou Keita, sanctions committee leader Michel Xavier Bang, the secretary-general of the East African Community and Rebecca Kabuo from LUCHA. Norway and others expressed grave concern over the situation and condemned all acts of violence by armed groups. Norway also called on all groups and countries to respect DR Congo s territorial integrity. Norway also praised and supported regional peace tracks and emphasised that the withdrawal of Monusco from DR Congo should take place based on the situation on the ground and not an artificially set timeline. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Meeting on Ukraine requested by Russia. Russia once again wanted to discuss what they refer to as the issue of supplies of lethal weapons to Ukraine and their consequences . Russia repeated well-known claims that arms to Ukraine contributed to increased conflict and escalation in the form of spreading to other conflict areas and to terrorist groups. Furthermore, they justified their own actions and attacks, accusing the West of prolonging the war and contributing to the killing of civilians. In line with like-minded countries, Norway condemned Russia s war of aggression and declared full support for Ukraine. Norway emphasised that Ukraine had the right to defend itself and to receive military support. Furthermore, Norway expressed deep concern over the increase in Russian attacks against the civilian population and infrastructure, including the use of Iranian drones in violation of Security Council Resolution 2231. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: New resolution adopted on humanitarian exemptions in UN sanctions regimes (resolution 2664). The resolution ensures that the UN's sanctions regimes do not entail unintended negative consequences for humanitarian work. Ensuring access for humanitarian aid and protecting civilians has been a priority for Norway in all discussions about UN sanctions regimes. Ireland and the USA initiated the resolution and Norway was a co-sponsor. The resolution was adopted with 14 votes in favour and one abstention (India). (MFA)

 

POLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS

ü  Labour/Centre Party still struggling: Ipsos party barometer poll for Dagbladet in December shows the Progress Party and Liberal Party falling and gains for the Centre Party and Socialist Left. The results are as follows (figures in parentheses show % change from last month): Red Party 6.3 (+0.4); Socialist Left 9.6 (+1.2); Labour 19.9 (+0.1); Centre Party 6.2 (+1.4); The Greens 4.1 (+0.8); KrF 3.4 (+0.3); Liberals 4.6 (-1.4); Conservatives 29.1 (-0.7); Progress Party 11.8 (-2.9); others 5.1 (+0.9). Based on this poll, the non-socialist parties would have a 92-seat majority if an election were held today. (DB 17/12 pp14-15 & 16)

 

NEWS IN BRIEF

*         King Harald admitted to hospital with an infection: The Royal Palace reports that HM King Harald has been admitted to the National Hospital diagnosed with an infection that needs to be treated with intravenous antibiotics. He will remain in hospital for a few days. His condition is stable. (nrk.no)

*         Statement by the Troika and EU on South Sudan: The MFA publishes a new statement by members of the Troika and the European Union on violence in Upper Nile and Jonglei States in South Sudan. Members of the Troika and EU are deeply concerned by an escalation in violence in Upper Nile and Jonglei, South Sudan, where there have been reports of scores of civilians killed and around 50,000 displaced. These reports of killings, homes and livelihoods burned and destroyed, and sexual and gender-based violence, including against minors, are horrifying and cannot go unaddressed. Read the full statement here in English. (MFA)

*         New travel advisory for Ethiopia: The MFA advises against all travel to the Tigray region of Ethiopia, as well as the border areas between the region of Amhara and Tigray, and the region of Afar and Tigray, the border areas with Sudan and Eritrea. The MFA also advises against all travel to the conflict-affected areas in western Ethiopia, including the areas of Kelam Welega, West Welega, Buno Bedele, East Welega, Horo Guduru Welega in Oromia Region, Gambela Region and Benishangul-Gumuz Region. The MFA advises against all travel to eastern parts of the Somali region and the border areas with Somalia. The MFA advises against all non-essential travel to other parts of Ethiopia. There is no travel advice for the capital Addis Ababa. (MFA)

*         Martine Vik Magnussen case: Dagbladet reported yesterday that the Yemeni authorities had issued a warrant for the arrest of Farouk Abdulhak, wanted by the British police in connection with the murder of Norwegian student Martine Vik Magnussen in London in 2008. Martine s father, Odd Petter Magnussen, who has been steadfast in seeking justice for his daughter, confirmed to NRK that he had received an email from the MFA informing him of the development. Shortly after Martine s murder,  Abdulhak, the son of a wealthy Yemini, fled London to Yemen. The UK does not have an extradition treaty with Yemen. (DB.no; nrk.no)

*         Sport and politics: Dagsavisen on Saturday commented that the FIFA World Cup in Qatar would be remembered for politics and other controversies, with the sport coming second. The newspaper urges a full and independent investigation into claims that as many as 6,500 guest workers have died building the stadiums and infrastructure for NOK 3 trillion. If the World Cup is awarded to Saudi Arabia in 2030, says the newspaper, it will show that FIFA s loyalty is with money and not with the ideals of football and its billions of fans. Meanwhile, NRK says it has been trying for the last 9 months to find out how FIFA president Gianni Infantino s Fifa Forward project works, albeit without success. (Da 17/12 pp4(leader), 26-31 & 47; nrk.no; Aft 19/12 pp44-45)

 

THE ECONOMY, TRADE AND INDUSTRY

 

COMMERCIAL NEWS ROUND-UP

*         Energy support package for industry: Trade & industry minister Jan Christian Vestre announced on Friday that almost 3,200 companies had qualified for a share of NOK 2.8bn allocated for energy saving measures and electricity subsidies before year-end. According to Vestre, an estimated 20,000 would qualify for support, but applications had only been received from 3,186 companies. Of these, 70% will invest in solar panels, heat exchangers, new windows, better insulation and other energy-saving measures. The Government estimates that the energy saved will equal the consumption of 30,000 households. Part of the package includes energy companies offering industry fixed-price contracts, something with the industry describes as an illusion . Meanwhile, Elkem has announced it is temporary closing part of its production in Norway due to high electricity prices. The decision involves the company s smelting furnaces at Thamshavn and Rana. (Aft 17/12 p34; e24.no; e24.no)

*         Household economy analysis: According to calculations by Nordea bank, an average household with two children will have its disposable income reduced by NOK 3,000 per month in 2023 due to rising interest rates, higher electricity rates and price inflation. The bank expects many to apply for relief on repayments of mortgages and consumption to fall (this has not happened yet, write Aftenposten and VG). Things will ease towards the end of the year, according to the analysis. (nrk.no; Aft 19/12 p10; VG 19/12 pp6-7 & 8)

The sensors to be upgraded are fitted on all-terrain vehicles and search for hostile threats in the air and on the ground, both in light and in the dark, using a TV camera and heat signature (infrared). The sensors also measure the distance to the target with a laser. The work to increase our national capacity against long-range precision weapons is ongoing and the modernisation of the current NASAMS is one of several measures aimed at strengthening Norway s air defence. The war in Ukraine has highlighted the need and importance of air defence. We have also recently signed a contract for the purchase of hand-held air defence weapons for the Army, to strengthen our ability to protect ourselves, says defence minister Bjørn Arild Gram. Upgraded sensors for the NASAMS will be continuously delivered to the Army and Air Force from the first half of 2025. (NMoD)

 

Q&A IN WESTERN SAHARA

Foreign minister Anniken Huitfeldt replies to written question no. 675 (2022-2023) from Freddy André Øvstegård (Socialist Left) on the Norwegian ship Heenvliet that was heading Western Sahara on charter (see PS of 9/12): Norway has officially advised against trade and other commercial activities in Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara since 2007, to prevent violations of international law, and in line with UN work to contribute to a solution to the conflict. Despite this, the Norwegian ship Heenvliet is on its way to Western Sahara with an estimated arrival of 11 December, according to Bergens Tidende of 8 December. What does the foreign minister think about such violations of official advice? Huitfeldt: The Norwegian authorities are keen to avoid actions that could be perceived as legitimising the situation in Western Sahara. Norway s precautionary stance is therefore firmly established. This is in the form of a general advice against trade, resource exploitation and other forms of business activity that are not in accordance with the interests of the Sahrawis and can consequently contribute to violations of international law. Morocco does not exercise internationally recognised sovereignty over Western Sahara, and thus does not have the right to exploit Western Sahara s natural resources as if they were their own. Our advice is a clear call to private actors to exercise caution and social responsibility when considering activity in the Western Sahara. It is also important to note that there is no legally binding ban on exports and commercial activities aimed at Western Sahara, nor UN sanctions or restrictive measures from the EU which involve export restrictions or other forms of restrictions related to commercial activities. (MFA)

 

MORE SUPPORT TO NATURE CONSERVATION

From the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in Montreal, climate & environment minister Espen Barth Eide announced that Norway was allocating a further NOK 120m to projects that will kick-start the implementation of a new nature agreement. The total funding needed to deliver on the global ambitions for the conservation and sustainable management of nature is estimated to be 5-8 times higher than current funding. In order to halt and reverse the loss of nature, there is therefore a need for significantly increased funding, both by countries stepping up their own efforts, and by banks, private companies and financial institutions contributing. In addition to new funding, environmentally damaging subsidies must be phased out, the Ministry says in a press release. (&).

Norway is the world s 5th largest country measured in aid to nature conservation. This includes the Norwegian rainforest initiative, in addition to aid for the conservation of marine areas and sustainable agriculture. Norway also puts considerable effort into mobilising funding from other countries, companies and the financial sector. An example of this is the mobilisation of USD 1.5bn for rainforest conservation through the LEAF coalition. If we are to solve the nature crisis, everyone must contribute more, including Norway. That is why the government will increase aid significantly until 2026, Barth Eide says. (&). (Press release; e24.no; Aft 19/12 p14)

 

WEEKLY REPORT ON NORWAY IN THE UN SECURITY COUNCIL

In week 49 the UN Security Council discussed: Iraq, Syria, DR Congo, Ukraine, Sudan, the Golan Heights, Central Africa, humanitarian exemptions in UN sanction regies.

Monday 5 December: Half-yearly meeting on UN ISIL investigation team (Unitad), with briefing by leader Christian Ritscher. Broad support for Unitad s core mandate, though some dissatisfaction that evidence has not been shared with the Iraqi authorities due to Iraqi laws and use of death sentence. Norway urged Iraq to temporarily suspend capital punishment in order to make progress. Norway also requested Unitad to continue prioritising the needs of survivors and to ensure an age and gender perspective in further work. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Open meeting and closed consultations on the elimination of Syria s chemical weapons programme. Read Norway s statement here.

6 December: Closed meeting with troop and police contributors to Monusco in DR Congo ahead of a mandate renewal later this month. Same day: Open meeting on the humanitarian situation in Ukraine called by France and Mexico. UN emergency aid coordinator Martin Griffiths painted a dire picture. Apart from Russia, members expressed considerable concern, particularly for the situation of children. Norway strongly condemned Russia s war of aggression with particular emphasis on the consequences of destroyed schools and health facilities for children and the Ukrainian civilian population. Norway also expressed concern about reports that Ukrainian children had been forcibly moved to Russia for adoption. Read Norway s statement here.

7 December: Open meeting and closed consultations on Sudan and Unitams, with briefing from the head of the sanctions committee for Sudan (1591), Ghana's UN ambassador, Agyeman. The meeting was characterised by new optimism after the civilian and military authorities in Sudan signed a new framework agreement on 5 December which may open up the formation of a new civilian government and a two-year transitional phase until the holding of democratic elections. Most of the council's members, including Norway, expressed concern that the humanitarian crisis in the country was worsening. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Closed meeting with troop and police contributors to Undof/Untso (Golan Heights). Norway supports Undof/Untso and the UN s role in continued monitoring of the ceasefire agreement.

8 December: Closed consultations on Undof (Golan Heights) before expected new mandate later this month. Same day: Half-yearly briefing and closed consultations on Unoca in Central Africa. Norway praised Unoca for its work and also expressed concern about the situation in eastern DR Congo, Chad and Cameroon, as well as about the food security situation in the region. Read Norway s statement here.

9 December: Meeting on the situation in DR Congo, Monusco and sanctions regime with briefings by UN special representative Bintou Keita, sanctions committee leader Michel Xavier Bang, the secretary-general of the East African Community and Rebecca Kabuo from LUCHA. Norway and others expressed grave concern over the situation and condemned all acts of violence by armed groups. Norway also called on all groups and countries to respect DR Congo s territorial integrity. Norway also praised and supported regional peace tracks and emphasised that the withdrawal of Monusco from DR Congo should take place based on the situation on the ground and not an artificially set timeline. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: Meeting on Ukraine requested by Russia. Russia once again wanted to discuss what they refer to as the issue of supplies of lethal weapons to Ukraine and their consequences . Russia repeated well-known claims that arms to Ukraine contributed to increased conflict and escalation in the form of spreading to other conflict areas and to terrorist groups. Furthermore, they justified their own actions and attacks, accusing the West of prolonging the war and contributing to the killing of civilians. In line with like-minded countries, Norway condemned Russia s war of aggression and declared full support for Ukraine. Norway emphasised that Ukraine had the right to defend itself and to receive military support. Furthermore, Norway expressed deep concern over the increase in Russian attacks against the civilian population and infrastructure, including the use of Iranian drones in violation of Security Council Resolution 2231. Read Norway s statement here. Same day: New resolution adopted on humanitarian exemptions in UN sanctions regimes (resolution 2664). The resolution ensures that the UN's sanctions regimes do not entail unintended negative consequences for humanitarian work. Ensuring access for humanitarian aid and protecting civilians has been a priority for Norway in all discussions about UN sanctions regimes. Ireland and the USA initiated the resolution and Norway was a co-sponsor. The resolution was adopted with 14 votes in favour and one abstention (India). (MFA)

He will remain in hospital for a few days. His condition is stable. (nrk.no)

Members of the Troika and EU are deeply concerned by an escalation in violence in Upper Nile and Jonglei, South Sudan, where there have been reports of scores of civilians killed and around 50,000 displaced. These reports of killings, homes and livelihoods burned and destroyed, and sexual and gender-based violence, including against minors, are horrifying and cannot go unaddressed. *         New travel advisory for Ethiopia: The MFA advises against all travel to the Tigray region of Ethiopia, as well as the border areas between the region of Amhara and Tigray, and the region of Afar and Tigray, the border areas with Sudan and Eritrea. The MFA also advises against all travel to the conflict-affected areas in western Ethiopia, including the areas of Kelam Welega, West Welega, Buno Bedele, East Welega, Horo Guduru Welega in Oromia Region, Gambela Region and Benishangul-Gumuz Region. *         Martine Vik Magnussen case: Dagbladet reported yesterday that the Yemeni authorities had issued a warrant for the arrest of Farouk Abdulhak, wanted by the British police in connection with the murder of Norwegian student Martine Vik Magnussen in London in 2008. Martine s father, Odd Petter Magnussen, who has been steadfast in seeking justice for his daughter, confirmed to NRK that he had received an email from the MFA informing him of the development. Shortly after Martine s murder,  Abdulhak, the son of a wealthy Yemini, fled London to Yemen. The UK does not have an extradition treaty with Yemen. (DB.no; nrk.no)

If the World Cup is awarded to Saudi Arabia in 2030, says the newspaper, it will show that FIFA s loyalty is with money and not with the ideals of football and its billions of fans. Meanwhile, NRK says it has been trying for the last 9 months to find out how FIFA president Gianni Infantino s Fifa Forward project works, albeit without success. (Da 17/12 pp4(leader), 26-31 & 47; nrk.no; Aft 19/12 pp44-45)

COMMERCIAL NEWS ROUND-UP

*         Energy support package for industry: Trade & industry minister Jan Christian Vestre announced on Friday that almost 3,200 companies had qualified for a share of NOK 2.8bn allocated for energy saving measures and electricity subsidies before year-end. According to Vestre, an estimated 20,000 would qualify for support, but applications had only been received from 3,186 companies. Of these, 70% will invest in solar panels, heat exchangers, new windows, better insulation and other energy-saving measures. The Government estimates that the energy saved will equal the consumption of 30,000 households. Part of the package includes energy companies offering industry fixed-price contracts, something with the industry describes as an illusion . Meanwhile, Elkem has announced it is temporary closing part of its production in Norway due to high electricity prices. The decision involves the company s smelting furnaces at Thamshavn and Rana. (Aft 17/12 p34; e24.no; e24.no)

*         Household economy analysis: According to calculations by Nordea bank, an average household with two children will have its disposable income reduced by NOK 3,000 per month in 2023 due to rising interest rates, higher electricity rates and price inflation. The bank expects many to apply for relief on repayments of mortgages and consumption to fall (this has not happened yet, write Aftenposten and VG). Things will ease towards the end of the year, according to the analysis. (nrk.no; Aft 19/12 p10; VG 19/12 pp6-7 & 8)
